ways.name: The shared Goode approach to 7,400 ft, then the talus cirque and the right-most notch
ways.season: Late July through September; snow often lingers in the basin above about 7,400 ft into early August, so carry an axe and consider crampons even for a nominally dry climb
ways.notes:
Storm King sits at the head of Thunder Creek and is one of the range's most remote summits — a three-day car-to-car trip is the norm, and three separate trailhead approaches converge on the same high basin below Goode's south side.

The most common is Thunder Creek: from Colonial Creek Campground on SR-20, the Thunder Creek trail roughly 13 miles with little gain to the McAllister Creek confluence, past Junction, Skagit Queen and Thunder Basin camps, then the Park Creek Pass trail junction and the switchbacks to Park Creek Pass. Alternatives are McAlester Pass and Rainbow Creek from SR-20, or a boat or shuttle to Stehekin and High Bridge Camp then the Park Creek trail from the south. From Stehekin the boot path starts on the north side of a large whitish-rock washout about two miles above the Two Mile camp, near 4,100 ft, five minutes further into the woods.

Every approach joins that trail: from Thunder Creek, cross Park Creek Pass and descend its south side to the washout. Leave the trail at the small cairn, climb the burned ridge beside the washout ravine, trend climber's left through heather and game trails, and follow cairns above about 6,500 ft to the basin below Goode at about 7,400 ft. From there, traverse snow and talus, favouring climber's left, roughly a mile to the cirque below Storm King's east and west towers. A rib camp around 7,450 ft with nearby water is the usual base.

From the cirque, a long and very loose talus and scree slope leads up toward the southwest gully system. Helmet on and space out — that slope is the approach's main hazard.

ways.name: Stehekin and the Park Creek trail
ways.notes: Take the boat up the lake to Stehekin and the shuttle to High Bridge, then walk up the valley past Bridge Creek to the Park Creek trail and climb it past Two Mile Camp. About a mile before Five Mile Camp, look for cairns marking a class 2-3 climbers' path up to the basin below Goode at about 7,400 ft. The least climbing of the three ways if the boat and shuttle schedule suits.

ways.name: Cascade Pass and the upper Stehekin valley
ways.notes: A drive-to start from the west side when the boat is impractical. Cross Cascade Pass and descend into the Stehekin valley, follow it down to the Park Creek trail, then climb Park Creek to the same cairned climbers' path up to the basin below Goode.

name: South Route

ways.name: Pete Lake and the PCT switchbacks to the Vista Lakes tarns
ways.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, but see the moat note — the gate at 7,000 ft can shut by mid-July, earlier in a thin snow year
ways.notes:
Walk the Pete Lake trail #1323 up the Cooper River to a fork at about 3,120 ft, roughly five miles in. Turn right, continue about six tenths of a mile, and turn right again onto the Pacific Crest Trail at about 3,220 ft. Follow the PCT four and a half miles up a long series of switchbacks to about 5,500 ft.

The Vista Lakes tarns lie east of the trail at that height and hold the good bivy sites. Summit Chief is about two more miles from there. Reported times from the car to the upper lake run to most of a day with overnight loads, and every published account treats this as a two- or three-day trip.

This is also the last reliable water. The ground above is reported bone dry until you come back down to the lakes.

From camp, leave the PCT and traverse cross-country toward Summit Chief Pass, then follow the ridge north-west staying below the cliffs and gendarmes, into the upper basin south-east of the main summit. One party's hindsight on this traverse is worth having: they should have dropped to about 6,000 ft and taken the scree instead of holding height across steep sloping slabs.

ways.name: Lemah Meadow shortcut, cutting the PCT switchbacks
ways.season: Same window; the bypass is brushier and is a trade of distance for thrashing
ways.notes: A recorded variant that saves about three miles. After gaining roughly a thousand feet on the tight PCT switchbacks, leave the trail at the corner around 4,000 ft and head north, climbing about six hundred feet to the crest. The party who did it found plenty of windfall and pockets of vine maple, and called it irritating rather than difficult. It is a single-source variant, so treat the line as a hint rather than a route.

priorPrimaryResearch: Paragraph describes Pete Lake and the PCT switchbacks to Vista Lakes (v0); v1 Lemah Meadow shortcut is a single-source brushy variant.

name: Standard Route (Southwest Face)

ways.name: The northern line: Access Creek and Luna Col, then the high traverse over Luna, East Fury and West Fury to the Swiss-Fury saddle
ways.notes:
From the Ross Dam Trailhead at milepost 134 on WA-20, about a mile of trail and service road drops to Ross Lake, crossed by the resort water taxi or by paddling or walking round. Pick up the Big Beaver Trail north along the lake and follow it roughly 10 miles to Luna Camp, then about 1.5 miles further to the Access Creek drainage.

Leave the trail and climb the brushy, moderately steep Access Creek valley, staying on its north side, to the open basin east of Luna Peak at about 4,300 ft. This is described as the easiest and least brushy approach on the east side of the Pickets. From there, gain Access Col and traverse cross-country and glaciated terrain over Luna Peak, East Fury and West Fury to reach the Swiss-Fury saddle.

ways.name: The southern line: Bacon Creek Road, Porkbelly and Mystery Ridges, Jasper Pass and Crowder's northeast ridge to Pickell Pass
ways.notes:
The alternate, and the shorter of the two in spirit if not in effort. It reaches Swiss from the south via Bacon Creek Road, Porkbelly Ridge, Mystery Ridge, Jasper Pass, Pioneer Ridge and Mount Crowder's northeast ridge, down to a camp at Pickell Pass.

This line is off-trail for most of its length, so treat the ridge sequence as the route rather than any particular tread.

priorPrimaryResearch: Big Beaver/Access Creek/Luna Col is the documented standard; variant 1 notes call the Bacon Creek line the alternate and off-trail, known only in outline.

ways.name: Foggy Dew Creek and Merchants Basin to Cooney Lake
ways.season: Mid-July to early October; larch Sep
ways.notes: Most parties backpack in and camp at one of the lakes rather than push the whole eighteen to twenty mile round trip in a day. From the Foggy Dew road end the trail climbs the North Fork past a two-tiered cascade — the last easy water before the country opens — and tops out of the timber into a wildflower basin below the ridge, where a spur trail branches toward the lake. An alternative comes in on the Crater Creek and Eagle Lake trail, taking a signed cutoff south past a second set of lakes to reach the same lake basin. Above the lake the ground is dry, so fill there. Larches turn gold around the basin in late September, which is a fine but colder window with a real chance of early snow icing the summit blocks.

ways.name: Crater Creek and the Eagle Lakes side
ways.notes: A higher start at about 4,760 ft and a gentler grade, with a creek ford. From the Crater Creek trailhead follow the Eagle Lakes trail a little over two miles, then the Martin Creek trail to the Cooney Lake trail; parties can also base at Upper Eagle Lake and cross Horsehead Pass. Often used to make a loop with the Foggy Dew side.

name: South Couloir (Standard Route)

ways.name: Lena Lake and the Brothers climbers' path (summer)
ways.season: Jun-Sep; by late August the couloir is often scrambling rather than snow
ways.notes:
Lena Lake Trailhead (Trail #810) off FS-25, around 700 ft. About 3 miles and 1,100 ft of gain on maintained trail through second- and old-growth, crossing several creek drainages, to Lena Lake at roughly 1,800 ft — a busy backpacking destination with a ranger station, and the last easy reliable water and camping before the climbers' route.

Skirt the west side of the lake and pick up the unmaintained but well-trodden Brothers boot path, which follows the East Fork Lena Creek drainage through the old-growth known as the Valley of the Silent Men for roughly 2.5-3 miles to a climbers' camp around 2,900 ft, marked by a fire ring. Most parties use this as high camp for a two-day ascent.

Route-finding gets hardest immediately after leaving camp for the summit push, where the boot path repeatedly appears to vanish. Follow a climbers' path upstream and west along the west fork for about a mile. It crosses an avalanche debris field where slide alder and downed logs — some with hand-lines or steps cut into them — hide the line, and creek fords may be needed. Beyond the debris field the path re-enters forest and climbs toward the couloir.

Water is reliable at the lake and up Lena Creek to high camp. Above camp there is nothing dependable once you are on scree and snow.

ways.name: Early-season snow ascent
ways.notes:
The classic time for this route is early season, roughly April into May, because the gullies fill in with dense brush later and the snow-covered version is much faster.

The approach is the same — Lena Lake, the Brothers boot path up the East Fork, the climbers' camp near 2,900 ft — but the avalanche debris field between camp and the couloir is easier under snow, and the couloir itself becomes a snow climb requiring an axe and reliable self-arrest rather than a scree slog.

Snow also buries the boot path, so the route-finding difficulty immediately above camp is worse, not better: there is no tread to find at all.

priorPrimaryResearch: Both variants follow the same Lena Lake approach. Variant 1's notes say early season is the classic time because the gullies brush in later, and most trip reports are spring/early summer on snow. The paragraph describes the summer boot path and debris field (variant 0).

name: The Scoop

ways.name: Colchuck Lake outlet into the west cirque
ways.notes:
Stuart Lake Trailhead (NF-7601 off Icicle Creek Road; Northwest Forest Pass). Stuart Lake Trail #1599 for roughly 2.25 miles with a Mountaineer Creek log bridge near 1.5 miles, to the junction where Colchuck Lake Trail #1599A branches left; a second Mountaineer Creek log crossing, then steepening rocky switchbacks to Colchuck Lake — about 4 miles and 2,280 ft, roughly one and three-quarter to two hours for a fit party.

The shorter line into the west basin: cross the lake's outlet below the small dam at the north end and follow the climbers' path up and across the timbered hillside straight into the cirque — about an hour from the lake, plus 15 to 25 minutes of boulder-hopping to the wall. Colchuck Lake is the last dependable water; carry what you need for a long day.

ways.name: Aasgard-side lakeshore, slide alder, leftmost gully
ways.season: Jul-Sep; ice axe useful before mid-July
ways.notes: Follow the lakeshore climbers' path counter-clockwise toward the Aasgard Pass slopes, gaining talus and heather about 400 ft above the lake, then cut north through the slide-alder band — cairned, but a genuine bushwhack of 15 to 20 minutes. Take the left-most gully and climb it about 1,000 ft to its top, then contour east on an easy path into the basin. One and a half to two hours from the lake, more gain than the outlet line but no ford.

priorPrimaryResearch: Prose presents both but calls the outlet line shorter (about an hour vs 1.5-2 h); the north-end outlet climbers' path is the usual way into the Colchuck Balanced Rock west cirque.

name: South Face (Standard)

ways.name: Snow Lake Trail to Great Scott Bowl and Pineapple Pass
ways.notes: Upper Alpental lot at the end of Alpental Road (about 3,100 ft), I-90 exit 52. Take the Snow Lake Trail (#1013) north; a cat track runs up the valley from the end of the lot, just left of the stream, before the tread narrows to normal trail. At roughly 1.5-1.6 miles a small signed junction splits Source Lake from Snow Lake — bear left toward Source Lake. Cross the Source Lake basin contouring near 4,000 ft, then at about 4,400 ft you crest a lip and drop into Great Scott Bowl (also called Pineapple Basin). Work up the bowl on talus, or on snow if any remains, toward Pineapple Pass at the head of it, passing beneath the Fang — the pinnacle on the bowl's west side that carries the Edge of Time route. The common error is here, not lower down: a boot path running around the back of the Fang leads into the gully between the Fang and the Tooth. Parties who take it have to backtrack several hundred feet through trees and rock fields to get back onto the right ground. The second error is going straight up to Pineapple Pass itself — that col is the rappel line down, not the way up.

ways.name: Winter and spring, snow-covered Alpental valley
ways.notes: Once there is meaningful snow the summer tread is not the route. The talus slopes the summer trail crosses are the Alpental valley's avalanche chutes — seventeen of them are counted along its length — and the winter line instead climbs the valley on the south side of the South Fork Snoqualmie toward Source Lake rather than following the summer switchbacks across those paths. From below Source Lake, traverse up into Great Scott Bowl, typically on an upward-traversing line on the west side of the bowl passing beneath the Fang, and join whatever track leads to Pineapple Pass. Most parties cache skis or snowshoes in the bowl before the final slope. The entire trip through the Source Lake and Snow Lake basins is avalanche terrain; this is a stability decision, not a route-finding one.

priorPrimaryResearch: Paragraph describes the summer Snow Lake trail / Source Lake / Great Scott Bowl approach (v0); v1 is the winter avalanche-terrain line with a different season.

name: South Peak via Lookout

ways.name: Tupso Pass trailhead, Trail #641 (road drivable)
ways.notes:
Trail #641 from the Tupso Pass trailhead at the end of FR 41. Forest to Saddle Lake at about two and a half miles — the last easy water, with no fires and no camping within two hundred feet of the shore beyond this point — then up through meadows to Goat Flats at roughly four and a half miles, which has the best camping on the route and views out to Puget Sound.

From Goat Flats the trail climbs about two more miles to Tin Can Gap at roughly six miles, banking most of the day's gain. That is the effective end of the maintained trail and where most walkers turn back.

The trail has been maintained by volunteers in recent years, with large numbers of logs cleared; note that a big fallen log above Saddle Lake has rerouted the tread, and there is a rough connector going straight up and down to the next switchback.

ways.name: Road-closure variation — walk or bike FR 41
ways.season: whenever the road is closed at the washout
ways.notes:
FR 41 is closed to vehicles at the washed-out Canyon Creek bridge, leaving roughly nine miles of road between the closure and the trailhead. Vehicles are barred past the barrier but foot and bike traffic are allowed, and biking the road is the common tactic.

Treat this as a standing possibility rather than a one-off: check with the Darrington Ranger District or the Verlot Public Service Center before committing, because the difference is a day hike versus an overnight. There is now a sign at the road marking the old trailhead.

priorPrimaryResearch: USFS: FR 41 is washed out and permanently closed to vehicles past Canyon Creek bridge, ~8-9 mi below the Tupso Pass trailhead; WTA Sept 2025 TR reports a dozen bikes at the bridge. So every party now walks/bikes the road; the prose assumes a drivable road.

ways.name: Surprise Creek past Surprise and Glacier lakes
ways.notes: The more popular way in, from a trailhead that is easy to find near Scenic on US 2. Climb the Surprise Creek trail to Surprise Lake, join the Pacific Crest Trail and follow it north to Trap Pass, then take the unofficial path south from the pass to the Thunder Mountain lakes basin under the north face.

ways.name: Tunnel Creek, Hope Lake and the PCT
ways.notes: From the Tunnel Creek trailhead off US 2, climb about a mile and a half to Hope Lake on the Pacific Crest Trail. Follow the PCT south a couple of miles over meadowy ground and up the switchbacks to Trap Pass, then take the unofficial path south to the Thunder Mountain lakes basin.

name: North Couloir

ways.name: Over the pass at the head of the river road, then east and down to the lake
ways.season: Spring into early summer, while the couloir still holds continuous snow
ways.notes:
From the trailhead at the end of the river road, climb to the pass at about 5,392 ft - or to the nearby col used as an alternative when the pass is corniced - and then travel east, descending and traversing through the basin beyond, to the lake at about 4,170 ft, which sits just north-east of the peak. From the lake you boot or skin directly to the foot of the route, changing to crampons or ascent plates as the snow firms up higher.

This is the approach that suits the route's season: the couloir is a snow line, so the party wants it early, which is also when the pass is a straightforward snow climb rather than a scramble.

ways.name: From the valley on the east, reaching the lake basin from below
ways.season: Summer, once the valley trail is open and the basin is snow-free enough to walk
ways.notes:
The lake basin can also be reached from the valley to the east, which is entered by boat or floatplane and then by road and trail up the valley floor. This is the approach the other route on this peak uses, and it puts a party at the lake without any pass to cross.

Treat the detail of it with caution. The published descriptions of this peak disagree about which drainage is followed off the valley trail and how far the lake is from the road, and the two accounts cannot both be right - so plan this variant from current maps and imagery rather than from a written description, and expect the off-trail section to be unmarked and steep.

priorPrimaryResearch: Over Cascade Pass/Alliteration Col suits the couloir's snow season. The Stehekin-side approach is used by the other route.

name: South Slopes

ways.name: Up the valley from the landing, then off-trail into the lake basin
ways.season: Midsummer through early autumn, once the basin is walkable and the valley road and trail are open
ways.notes:
There is no road to this side of the peak. Reach the valley by ferry or floatplane, then take the valley road or the park shuttle to a campground and pick up the valley trail from there. The lake below the peak is reached by leaving that trail and pushing off-trail and unmarked into the basin - a steep, poorly marked fisherman's path at best, and map-and-compass travel above it. Figure a full day of travel each way and plan on two or three days with a camp at or below the lake.

The off-trail departure is not well defined; plan it from current maps and imagery before you go.

ways.name: Over the pass at the head of the river road and down to the lake from the west
ways.season: Late spring into summer, while the pass is straightforward and the basin beyond is still simple travel
ways.notes:
The lake can also be reached from the other side of the range, by climbing to the pass at about 5,392 ft at the head of the river road - or the nearby col used when the pass is corniced - and then travelling east, descending and traversing through the basin beyond to the lake at about 4,170 ft.

This avoids the ferry and the unmarked valley push entirely, at the cost of a pass crossing in each direction and a descent that has to be re-climbed at the end of the trip.

priorPrimaryResearch: Trip reports (WTA 2019 Trapper Lake; Engineered for Adventure via Cascade River Road) reach Trapper Lake from Cascade Pass/Pelton Basin (5,392 ft pass = Cascade Pass), i.e. variant 1. Variant 0/prose's Stehekin ferry + Harlequin start is doubtful (Harlequin is far down-valley and variant 0's own notes flag conflicting drainages/distances).

ways.name: Goat Pass and the Stuart Glacier to the fourth-class gully and the notch
ways.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; earlier the gully to the notch holds snow and the glacier crossing is simpler, later it is bare and looser
ways.notes:
From the Esmeralda Basin trailhead at the end of the North Fork Teanaway Road, take the Ingalls Way trail over Ingalls Pass, past Ingalls Lake toward Stuart Pass, then the climbers' path onto the talus shoulder under Stuart's West Ridge and northwest to Goat Pass at about 7,600 ft.

From Goat Pass, traverse onto and across the Stuart Glacier rather than along beneath it, aiming for a fourth-class gully that runs up to the obvious notch in the North Ridge. This is the difference between this route and the complete ridge in one sentence: the complete-ridge party traverses east below the glacier to the toe, this party crosses the glacier and goes up.

The notch is a bivy: there are two good sites in it, which is why parties who intend to climb the upper ridge in a day from a high camp use it.

Published descriptions of this route are frank that the last of the navigation is yours — one of them says outright to take a topographic map and work it out. Treat that as a real warning rather than as rhetoric.

ways.name: Mountaineer Creek and the Stuart Glacier from the north
ways.notes: From the Stuart Lake trailhead, follow the trail up Mountaineer Creek, then leave it for the climbers' path into the basin below the Stuart and Sherpa glaciers. Climb the Stuart Glacier to the notch where the upper ridge begins. This suits parties camping in the north-side basin, but leaves the car on the opposite side from the Cascadian Couloir descent.
